'''abucco''' (a-bu̇k′kō), ''n.'' [A native term.] A weight nearly equal to half a pound avoirdupois, used in Burma.

'''abulia''' (a-bö′li-ä̤), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀβουλία, ill-advisedness, thoughtlessness, < ἄβουλος, ill-advised, thoughtless, < ἀ- priv. + βουλή, advice, counsel.] A form of mental derangement in which volition is impaired or lost. Also written ''aboulia''.

'''abulomania''' (a-bö-lọ̄-mā′ni-ä̤), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἄβουλος, ill-advised, thoughtless, + μανία, madness.] Same as ''abulia''. Also written ''aboulomania''.

'''abumbral''' (ab-um′bra̤l), ''a.'' Same as ''abumbrellar''.

'''abumbrellar''' (ab-um-brel′är), ''a.'' [< L. ''ab'', from, + NL. ''umbrella'', the disk of acalephs.] Turned away from the umbrella or disk: applied to the surface of the velum or marginal ridge of medusæ or sea-blubbers, and opposed to ''adumbrellar'' (which see).

'''abuna''' (a-bö′nä̤), ''n.'' [Ethiopic and Ar. ''abū-na'', our father. Cf. ''abba''.] The head of the Christian church in Abyssinia. See ''Abyssinian''.

'''abundance''' (ạ-bun′dans), ''n.'' [< ME. ''abundance'', ''habundaunce'', ''aboundance'' (see ''aboundance''), < OF. ''abondance'', < L. ''abundantia'', abundance, < ''abundare'', abound: see ''abound''.] '''1.''' A copious supply or quantity; overflowing plenteousness; unrestricted sufficiency: strictly applicable to quantity only, but sometimes used of number: as, an ''abundance'' of corn, or of people; to have money in great ''abundance''.
{{smaller block|By reason of the ''abundance'' of his horses their dust}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|abucco|26|abut}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''abucco''' (a-bu̇k′kō), ''n.''  [A native term.]  A weight nearly equal to half a pound avoirdupois, used in Burma.

'''abulia''' (a-bö′li-ä̤), ''n.''  [NL., < Gr. ἀβουλία, ill-advisedness, thoughtlessness, < ἄβουλος, ill-advised, thoughtless, < ἀ- priv. + βουλή, advice, counsel.]  A form of mental derangement in which volition is impaired or lost. Also written ''aboulia''.

'''abulomania''' (a-bö-lọ̄-mā′ni-ä̤), ''n.''  [NL., < Gr. ἄβουλος, ill-advised, thoughtless, + μανία, madness.]  Same as ''abulia''. Also written ''aboulomania''.

'''abumbral''' (ab-um′bra̤l), ''a.'' Same as ''abumbrellar''.

'''abumbrellar''' (ab-um-brel′är), ''a.''  [< L. ''ab'', from, + NL. ''umbrella'', the disk of acalephs.]  Turned away from the umbrella or disk: applied to the surface of the velum or marginal ridge of medusæ or sea-blubbers, and opposed to ''adumbrellar'' (which see).

'''abuna''' (a-bö′nä̤), ''n.''  [Ethiopic and Ar. ''abū-na'', our father. Cf. ''abba''.]  The head of the Christian church in Abyssinia. See ''Abyssinian''.

'''abundance''' (ạ-bun′dans), ''n.''  [< ME. ''abundance'', ''habundaunce'', ''aboundance'' (see ''aboundance''), < OF. ''abondance'', < L. ''abundantia'', abundance, < ''abundare'', abound: see ''abound''.]  '''1.''' A copious supply or quantity; overflowing plenteousness; unrestricted sufficiency: strictly applicable to quantity only, but sometimes used of number: as, an ''abundance'' of corn, or of people; to have money in great ''abundance''.
{{smaller block|By reason of the ''abundance'' of his horses their dust shall cover thee.{{right|Ezek. xxvi. 10.}}}}

'''2.''' Overflowing fullness or affluence; repletion; amplitude of means or resources.
{{smaller block|Out of the ''abundance'' of the heart the mouth speaketh.{{right|Mat. xii. 34.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''abundance'' [of Chaucer] is a continual fulness within the fixed limits of good taste; that of Langland is squandered in overflow.{{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 260.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Exuberance'', ''Profusion'', etc. (see ''plenty''); plenteousness, plentifulness, plenitude, sufficiency, copiousness, ampleness, luxuriance, supply. See ''affluence''.}}

'''abundancy†''' (a̤-bun′dạn-si), ''n.'' The state or quality of being abundant.

'''abundant''' (a̤-bun′dạnt), ''a.''  [< ME. ''abundant'', ''habundant'', ''aboundant'', < OF. ''abondant'', ''habondant'', < L. ''abundan(t-)s'', ppr. of ''abundare'', overflow: see ''abound''.]  '''1.''' Plentiful; present in great quantity; fully sufficient: as, an ''abundant'' supply.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy ''abundant'' goodness shall excuse
This deadly blot in thy digressing son.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., v. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|The history of our species is a history of the evils that have flowed from a source as tainted as it is ''abundant''.{{right|''Brougham.''}}}}
'''2.''' Possessing in great quantity; copiously supplied; having great plenty; abounding: followed by ''in''.
{{smaller block|The Lord, . . . ''abundant in'' goodness and truth.{{right|Ex. xxxiv. 6.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Abundant definition.''' See ''definition''.—'''Abundant number''', in ''arith.'', a number the sum of whose aliquot parts exceeds the number itself. Thus, 12 is an abundant number, for the sum of its aliquot parts (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6) is 16. It is thus distinguished from a ''perfect'' number, which is equal to the sum of all its aliquot parts, as 6 = 1 + 2 + 3; and from a ''deficient'' number, which is greater than the sum of all its aliquot parts, as 14, which is greater than 1 + 2 + 7. = '''Syn.''' Plentiful, plenteous, copious, ample, exuberant, lavish, overflowing, rich, large, great, bountiful, teeming. See ''ample''.}}

'''abundantly''' (a-bun′dant-li), ''adv.'' In a plentiful or sufficient degree; fully; amply; plentifully.

'''abune''' (a-bön′; Scotch pron. a-bün′), ''adv.'' and ''prep.''  [Contr. < ME. ''abuven'', ''aboven'' (pron. ä-bö′ven), < AS. ''ābufan'': see ''above''.]  Above; beyond; in a greater or higher degree. Also written ''aboon''. [Scotch.]

'''ab urbe condita''' (ab ėr′bē kon′di-tä).  [L.; lit., from the city founded: ''ab'', from; ''urbe'', abl. of ''urbs'', city; ''condita'', fem. pp. of ''condere'', put together, establish.]  From the founding of the city, that is, of Rome, {{sc|b. c.}} 753, the beginning of the Roman era. Usually abbreviated to ''A. U. C.'' (which see). {{img float|file=century v01 p0052 c1f1.png|width=183px|align=right|cap={{smaller|''Aburria carunculata.''}}}}

'''Aburria''' (a-bur′i-ä̤), ''n.''  [NL.; of S. Amer. origin.]  A genus of guans, of which the type is the wattled guan, ''Penelope aburri'' or ''Aburria carunculata'', of South America.  ''Reichenbach'', 1853.

'''aburton''' (a-bėr′to̤n), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''burton'': see ''burton''.]  ''Naut.'', placed athwartships in the hold: said of casks.

'''abusable''' (a-bū′za-bl), ''a.''  [< ''abuse'' + ''-able''.]  Capable of being abused.

'''abusage†''' (a-bū′zạ̄j), ''n.'' Same as ''abuse''.

'''abuse''' (a-būz′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''abused'', ppr. ''abusing''.  [< ME. ''abusen'', < OF. ''abuser'' (F. ''abuser''), < ML. ''abusari'', freq. of L. ''abūti'', pp. ''abūsus'', use up, consume, misuse, abuse, < ''ab'', from, mis-, + ''uti'', use: see ''use'', ''v.'']  '''1.''' To use ill; misuse; put to a wrong or bad use; divert from the proper use; misapply: as, to ''abuse'' rights or privileges; to ''abuse'' words.
{{smaller block|They that use this world as not ''abusing'' it. {{right|1 Cor. vii. 31.}}}}
{{smaller block|The highest proof of virtue is to possess boundless power without ''abusing'' it. {{right|''Macaulay'', Addison.}}}}
'''2.''' To do wrong to; act injuriously toward; injure; disgrace; dishonor.
{{smaller block|<poem>I swear, 'tis better to be much ''abus’d''
Than but to know’t a little.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Poor soul, thy face is much ''abused'' with tears. {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iv. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' To violate; ravish; defile.—'''4.''' To attack with contumelious language; revile.—'''5.''' To deceive; impose on; mislead.
{{smaller block|You are a great deal ''abused'' in too bold a persuasion. {{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, i. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|Nor be with all these tempting words ''abused''. {{right|''Pope'', tr. of Ovid, Sappho to Phaon, l. 67.}}}}
{{smaller block|It concerns all who think it worth while to be in earnest with their immortal souls not to ''abuse'' themselves with a false confidence, a thing so easily taken up, and so hardly laid down.
{{right|''South.''}}}}

{{smaller block|='''Syn. 1.''' To ''Abuse, Misuse'', misapply, misemploy, pervert, profane. ''Abuse'' and ''misuse'' are closely synonymous terms, but ''misuse'' conveys more particularly the idea of using inappropriately, ''abuse'' that of treating injuriously. In general, ''abuse'' is the stronger word.}}
{{smaller block|So a fool is one that hath lost his wisdom, . . . not one that wants reason, but ''abuses'' his reason.
{{right|''Charnock'', Attributes.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>From out the purple grape
Crushed the sweet poison of ''misused'' wine.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 47.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''2.''' To maltreat, ill-use, injure.—'''4.''' To revile, reproach, vilify, rate, berate, vituperate, rail at.}}

'''abuse''' (a-būs′), ''n.''  [= F. ''abus'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''abuso'', < L. ''abūsus'', a using up, < ''abūti'', pp. ''abūsus'', use up, misuse: see ''abuse'', ''v.'']  '''1.''' Ill use; improper treatment or employment; application to a wrong purpose; improper use or application: as, an ''abuse'' of our natural powers; an ''abuse'' of civil rights, or of religious privileges; ''abuse'' of advantages; ''abuse'' of words.
{{smaller block|<poem>Perverts best things
To worst ''abuse'', or to their meanest use.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 204.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And thus he bore without ''abuse''
The grand old name of gentleman.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, cx.}}}}
{{smaller block|A darling ''abuse'' of the liberty of conscience.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker.}}}}
'''2.''' Ill treatment of a person; injury; insult; dishonor; especially, ill treatment in words; contumelious language. {{smaller block|<poem>I, dark in light, exposed
To daily fraud, contempt, ''abuse'', and wrong.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 76.}}}}
'''3.''' A corrupt practice or custom; an offense; a crime; a fault: as, the ''abuses'' of government.
{{smaller block|The poor ''abuses'' of the time want countenance.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|If ''abuses'' be not remedied, they will certainly increase.
{{right|''Swift'', Adv. of Relig.}}}}
'''4.''' Violation; defilement: as, self-''abuse''.—'''5†.''' Deception.
{{smaller block|This is a strange ''abuse''.—Let’s see thy face.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Is it some ''abuse'', or no such thing?
{{right|''Shak.'', Ham., iv. 7.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Abuse of distress''', in ''law'', use of an animal or chattel distrained, which makes the distrainer liable to prosecution as for wrongful appropriation.—'''Abuse of process''', in ''law''. (''a'') Intentional irregularity for the purpose of gaining an advantage over one’s opponent. (''b'') More commonly, the use of legal process (it may be in a manner formally regular) for an illegal purpose; a perversion of the forms of law, as making a criminal complaint merely to coerce payment of a debt, or wantonly selling very valuable property on execution in order to collect a trifling sum.}}

{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' Misuse, perversion, profanation, prostitution.—'''3.''' ''Abuse, Invective'', maltreatment, outrage; vituperation, contumely, scolding, reviling, aspersion, slander, obloquy. (See ''invective''.) "''Abuse'' as compared with ''invective'' is more personal and coarse, being conveyed in harsh and unseemly terms, and dictated by angry feeling and bitter temper. ''Invective'' is more commonly aimed at character or conduct, and may be conveyed in writing and in refined language, and dictated by indignation against what is in itself blameworthy. It often, however, means public abuse under such restraints as are imposed by position and education." ''C. J. Smith.''}}

'''abuseful''' (a̤-būs′fu̇l), ''a.'' Using or practising abuse; abusive. [Rare or obsolete.]
{{smaller block|The ''abuseful'' names of hereticks and schismaticks.
{{right|''Bp. Barlow'', Remains, p. 397.}}}}

'''abuser''' (a̤-bū′zėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who abuses, in speech or behavior; one who deceives.
{{smaller block|Next thou, th' ''abuser'' of thy prince’s ear.
{{right|''Sir J. Denham'', Sophy.}}}}
'''2.''' A ravisher.
{{smaller block|That vile ''abuser'' of young maidens.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shep., v. 1.}}}}

'''abusion†''' (a̤-bū′zho̤n), ''n.''  [< ME. ''abusion'', < OF. ''abusion'' = Pr. ''abuzio'' = Sp. ''abusion'' = Pg. ''abusão'' = It. ''abusione'', < L. ''abusio(n-)'', misuse, in rhet. catachresis, < ''abūti'', pp. ''abūsus'', misuse: see ''abuse'', ''v.'']  '''1.''' Misuse; evil or corrupt usage; violation of right or propriety.
{{smaller block|Redress the ''abusions'' and exactions.
{{right|''Act of Parl.'' No. xxxiii. (23 Hen. VIII.).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Shame light on him, that through so false illusion,
Doth turne the name of Souldiers to ''abusion''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale, l. 220.}}}}
'''2.''' Reproachful or contumelious language; insult.—'''3.''' Deceit; illusion.
{{smaller block|They speken of magic and ''abusion''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Man of Law’s Tale, l. 116.}}}}

'''abusive''' (a̤-bū′siv), ''a.''  [= F. ''abusif'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''abusivo'', < L. ''abūsīvus'', misapplied, improper, < ''abūti'', pp. ''abūsus'', misuse: see ''abuse'', ''v.'']  '''1.''' Practising abuse; using harsh words or ill treatment: as, an ''abusive'' author; an ''abusive'' fellow.—'''2.''' Characterized by or containing abuse; marked by contumely or ill use; harsh; ill-natured; injurious.
{{smaller block|An ''abusive'', scurrilous style passes for satire, and a dull scheme of party notions is called fine writing.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 125.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>One from all Grub-street will my fame defend,
And, more ''abusive'', calls himself my friend.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Prol. to Satires, l. 112.}}}}
'''3.''' Marked by or full of abuses; corrupt: as, an ''abusive'' exercise of power.
{{smaller block|A very extensive and zealous party was formed [in France], which acquired the appellation of the Patriotic party, who, sensible of the ''abusive'' government under which they lived, sighed for occasions of reforming it.
{{right|''Jefferson'', Autobiog., p. 56.}}}}
'''4'''†. Misleading, or tending to mislead; employed by misuse; improper.
{{smaller block|In describing these battles, I am, for distinction sake, necessitated to use the word Parliament improperly, according to the ''abusive'' acception thereof for these latter years.
{{right|''Fuller'', Worthies, I. xviii.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1''' and '''2.''' Insolent, insulting, offensive, scurrilous, ribald, reproachful, opprobrious, reviling.}}

'''abusively''' (a-bū′siv-li), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In an abusive manner; rudely; reproachfully.—'''2'''†. Improperly; by misuse.
{{smaller block|Words being carelessly and ''abusively'' admitted, and as inconstantly retained.
{{right|''Glanville'', Van. of Dogmat., xvii.}}}}

'''abusiveness''' (a-bū′siv-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being abusive; rudeness of language, or violence to the person; ill usage.

'''abut''' (a̤-but′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''abutted'', ppr. ''abutting''.  [< ME. ''abutten'', ''abouten'', < OF. ''abouter'', ''abuter'', abut (F. ''abouter'', join end to end), < ''a'', to, + ''bout'', ''but'', end; cf. OF. ''boter'', F. ''bouter'', thrust, push, butt: see ''butt''<sup>1</sup>. The mod. F. ''aboutir'', arrive at, tend to, end in, depends in most of its senses upon ''bout'', an end, though strictly it represents the OF. ''abouter'', in the sense of ‘thrust toward.’]  '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To touch at the end; be contiguous; join at a border or boundary; terminate; rest: with ''on'', ''upon'', or ''against'' before the object: as, his land ''abuts upon'' mine; the building ''abuts on'' the highway; the bridge ''abuts against'' the solid rock.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whose high upreared and ''abutting'' fronts
The perilous, narrow ocean parts asunder.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., i. (cho.).}}}}
{{smaller block|Steam is constantly issuing in jets from the bottom of a small ravine-like hollow, which has no exit, and which ''abuts against'' a range of trachytic mountains.
{{right|''Darwin'', Geol. Observations, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|In the last resort all these questions of physical speculation ''abut upon'' a metaphysical question.
{{right|''W. K. Clifford'', Lectures, I. 243.}}}}
{{smaller block|The lustrous splendor of the walls ''abutting upon'' the Grand Canal. {{right|''D. G. Mitchell'', Bound Together, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''ship-building'', same as ''butt''<sup>1</sup>, 3.—'''Abutting owner''', {{smaller|an owner of land which abuts or joins. Thus, the owner of land bounded by a highway or river, or by a tract of land belonging to another person, is said in reference to the latter to be an ''abutting owner''. The term}} usually implies that the relative parts actually adjoin, but is sometimes loosely used without implying more than close proximity.—'''Abutting power''' (in an active sense), the ability of an abutment to resist the thrust or strain of the arch, gas, fluid, etc., pressing or reacting against it.—'''Abutting joint.''' See ''abutment'', 2 (''b'') (2).<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
